report:
## Conclusion: The Evidence Does Not Support a Link Between Childhood Vaccines and Autism

Your skepticism is well-founded. The overwhelming scientific consensus, based on large-scale studies across millions of children in multiple countries, is that **childhood vaccines do not cause autism**, and increasing the number of vaccines does not increase autism risk.

### Key Evidence

1. **The original claim was based on a fraudulent, retracted study.** A 1998 paper by Andrew Wakefield describing 12 children who received the MMR vaccine and later developed autism planted the seeds of doubt. The paper was retracted for fraud, and subsequent large studies found no association ([Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health](https://publichealth.jhu.edu/2025/vaccines-do-not-cause-autism)).

2. **Multiple large studies and meta-analyses find no causal link.** The WHO's Global Advisory Committee on Vaccine Safety concluded in 2025 that no causal link exists between vaccines and autism spectrum disorder ([WHO](https://www.who.int/news/item/11-12-2025-who-expert-group-s-new-analysis-reaffirms-there-is-no-link-between-vaccines-and-autism); [JAMA](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2843817)). A CDC study specifically examined whether "too many vaccines" increase autism risk and found no link ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/healthmain/new-study-finds-no-link-between-too-many-vaccines-autism-1c9139290)).

3. **Specific ingredients like thimerosal have been ruled out.** Research shows thimerosal, a mercury-based preservative, does not cause autism. When MMR and thimerosal hypotheses failed, alternative theories shifted but were also unsupported ([CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/vaccine-safety/about/autism.html); [PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2908388/)).

4. **The rise in autism prevalence is explained by other factors.** Researchers attribute the increase to greater awareness, improved screening, broadened diagnostic criteria, and changes in how autism is classified — not vaccines ([AAP](https://www.aap.org/en/news-room/fact-checked/fact-checked-vaccines-safe-and-effect-no-link-to-autism/); [Stanford Magazine](https://stanfordmag.org/contents/why-the-increase-no-it-s-not-vaccines)).

### Note on Conflicting Sources
Some websites (e.g., Children's Health Defense) cite studies claiming a vaccine-autism link. However, these studies are generally small, methodologically flawed, and not replicated by independent research. The *New York Times* analysis found that of 69 studies examined, 43 found no connection, and many of the 26 that did had significant methodological problems ([NYT](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2025/08/19/opinion/vaccines-autism-evidence.html)).
